en: To drive people away so they feel unwelcome or shut out
hook: ALIEN-ATE: makes you feel like an ALIEN.
story: Alienate. After scoring 330, Rafi could not stop talking about it. In the study group, he corrected everyone, laughed at wrong answers, and reminded people of his score twice a day. One by one, his friends stopped inviting him. By the end of the month, he was studying alone, wondering why. He had alienated them: made them feel unwelcome and turned them against him. Think: he made himself an alien among friends.

gre.s: The senator's harsh remarks about immigrants threatened to ____ the very voters whose support she needed to win reelection.
gre.clue: the very voters whose support she needed

example: The café's sudden price rise alienated the students who had been its most loyal customers for years.

en: Hostile and aggressive; eager to fight
story: Belligerent. At the bank, the queue moved slowly. One customer started muttering, then shouting, then slammed his fist on the counter and threatened to smash the glass if he was not served immediately. The terrified cashier pressed the alarm, and security guards escorted him out. He was belligerent: hostile, aggressive, eager to fight. Belli means war, as in rebellion. Belligerent nations are those at war. A belligerent tone turns any conversation into a battle.

gre.s: The diplomat's ____ remarks, which included open threats of military action, alarmed even his own government's allies.
gre.clue: open threats of military action

example: After losing the toss, the belligerent captain argued with the umpire so loudly that play was delayed for twenty minutes.

en: Twisted and so complicated that it is hard to follow
hook: CONVOLUTED: like a coiled-up VOLUTE, twisted spiral.
story: Convoluted. The new tax form had forty pages. Section B told you to see Section F, which sent you back to Section A, unless you were married, in which case you should consult Appendix Twelve, which did not exist. Even professional accountants gave up and laughed. The process was convoluted: extremely complex and twisted, hard to follow. A convoluted plot, convoluted reasoning, convoluted sentences. On the GRE, break convoluted sentences into small pieces.

gre.s: Students found the professor's lectures maddeningly ____, as each explanation looped through so many digressions that the main point was lost.
gre.clue: looped through so many digressions

example: The film's convoluted plot, with three timelines and two sets of twins, left most of the audience lost by the interval.

en: Marked by moral decline and excessive self-indulgence
story: Decadent. In the final years of the empire, the nobles threw parties that lasted for days. Golden plates. Rivers of wine. Musicians playing until dawn. Meanwhile, outside the palace walls, farmers starved and soldiers went unpaid. Within a decade, the empire collapsed. Historians describe that court as decadent: marked by moral decline and excessive indulgence in luxury. Decadent shares a root with decay. Today people jokingly call a rich chocolate cake decadent.

gre.s: Moralists of the era denounced the city's nightlife as ____, a sign that luxury and pleasure had corrupted the nation's character.
gre.clue: luxury and pleasure had corrupted the nation's character

example: Critics called the tycoon's gold-plated birthday cake decadent at a time when millions in the country could barely afford rice.

en: To move away from the usual path, plan, or rule
story: Deviate. Every morning, Zayan's father drives the same route to his office in Motijheel: same roads, same turns, same tea stall. One day a procession blocked the main road, and he was forced to deviate from his route, taking narrow lanes he had never seen. To deviate is to depart from an established course or norm. Statisticians measure standard deviation: how far values stray from the average. A deviant is someone who departs from social norms. Synonyms: diverge, stray, digress.

gre.s: Investigators concluded that the accident occurred because the crew chose to ____ from standard procedures, skipping two of the required safety checks before takeoff.
gre.clue: skipping two of the required safety checks

example: Whenever the professor deviated from her notes, the lecture grew livelier, full of stories from her fieldwork in the haor wetlands.

en: Using dishonest or tricky methods to achieve goals
story: Devious. Mahin wanted to be class representative. Instead of campaigning honestly, he created fake accounts to spread rumours about his rival, promised different things to different groups, and quietly bribed two students with free lunches. When the truth came out, everyone called him devious: using dishonest or tricky methods to achieve his goals. Devious literally means off the main road, from de, away, and via, way. A devious path winds and wanders. Synonyms: deceitful, cunning, underhanded, sly.

gre.s: Unable to win the contract fairly, the company resorted to ____ tactics, secretly leaking false information about its competitors to the press.
gre.clue: secretly leaking false information

example: In a devious move, the company changed its refund policy late on a Friday night, hoping customers would not notice until too late.

en: To spread information or ideas widely
hook: DIS-SEMIN-ate: 'semin' is Latin for seed. Scattering seeds in every direction.
story: Disseminate. At nine in the evening, the university quietly moved the final exam forward by one week. By nine thirty, the student union had disseminated the news everywhere: Facebook posts, WhatsApp groups, phone calls, and notices taped to every hostel door. By midnight, even students in distant villages knew. To disseminate is to spread information widely, the way a farmer scatters seeds across a whole field so they land everywhere at once.

gre.s: Public health officials worked to ____ accurate information about the virus as quickly as rumors were spreading online.
gre.clue: as quickly as rumors were spreading

example: Community radio stations along the coast disseminate cyclone warnings in local dialects so that fishermen understand them quickly.

en: Threats or force used to make someone do something
story: Duress. A small shop owner in Old Dhaka signed a paper giving away his land. Months later, in court, he explained that local thugs had stood behind him and threatened his family while he signed. The judge cancelled the contract, because it had been signed under duress: under threats or force. Duress comes from a Latin word for hard, like durable and endure: duress is hard pressure. The usual phrase is under duress. Synonyms: coercion, compulsion, intimidation.

gre.s: The judge ruled the confession inadmissible because it had been obtained under ____: the suspect had been threatened and denied sleep for three days.
gre.clue: had been threatened and denied sleep for three days

example: Hostages who praised their captors in a video later explained that they had spoken under duress.

en: Believing in equal rights and opportunities for all people
hook: EGALITARIAN: EGAL means equal in French (égal).
story: Egalitarian. At Kamal's new workplace, the chief executive eats lunch at the same table as the cleaners, everyone uses first names, and salaries are published openly so that men and women receive equal pay for equal work. Kamal had never seen an office so egalitarian: believing in equal rights and opportunities for all people. The word comes from the French egal, meaning equal. Its opposites are elitist and hierarchical. Synonyms: equitable, democratic, fair.

gre.s: Although the society claimed to be ____, its rigid caste system ensured that wealth and power remained in the hands of a few families.
gre.clue: its rigid caste system ensured

example: The village cooperative is strikingly egalitarian, giving every member one vote no matter how much land or money they bring.

en: Avoiding giving a clear, straight answer
bn: এড়িয়ে যাওয়া; ধরা দেয় না এমন
story: Evasive. Mitu came home at midnight. Her mother was waiting. "Where were you?" "Oh, around." "Around where?" "With friends." "Which friends?" "Just… people. Doing stuff." Her mother narrowed her eyes. Every answer had slid away from the question. Mitu was being evasive: avoiding direct answers or commitment. Evasive means tending to evade, to dodge. Evasive action is a manoeuvre to avoid danger, like a pilot steering around a storm.

gre.s: When asked directly about the missing funds, the treasurer grew ____, changing the subject and answering questions nobody had asked.
gre.clue: changing the subject and answering questions nobody had asked

example: My little brother turns evasive whenever Ammu asks about his homework, suddenly eager to discuss football or the weather.

en: To make something happen faster
hook: EXPEDITE: as fast as an EXPRESS delivery.
story: Expedite. Sara's visa interview was scheduled for three months away, but her classes in Germany started in one. Panicking, she paid an extra fee and submitted proof of her start date. The embassy expedited her application, and she had her appointment within ten days. To expedite is to make something happen faster. Expedited shipping costs more but arrives sooner. Think: as fast as an express train.

gre.s: To ____ the relief effort, the government waived the usual customs inspections for shipments of food and medicine.
gre.clue: waived the usual customs inspections

example: A new online system has expedited passport renewals, cutting the wait from several months to a few weeks.

en: Having or showing intense passion
story: Fervent. Every evening during the election season, Babu's uncle stood at the village tea stall, arguing passionately for his candidate. He printed posters with his own money, walked miles to rallies, and could recite every campaign promise from memory. He was a fervent supporter: full of intense passion. Fervent comes from a Latin word meaning to boil, the same root as fervour. A fervent prayer is one said with burning sincerity. Synonyms: ardent, zealous, passionate.

gre.s: Though once a ____ supporter of the policy, attending every rally and writing letters to every newspaper, he became its harshest critic after seeing its effects.
gre.clue: attending every rally and writing letters to every newspaper

example: A fervent believer in public libraries, the retired teacher gave her entire collection of three thousand books to the town of Jashore.

en: Strong, burning enthusiasm or emotion
story: Fervor. On Victory Day, sixteenth of December, thousands gathered at the National Memorial at dawn. When the national anthem began, the whole crowd sang together, voices rising, many with tears running down their faces, holding small flags high. The passion in the air was electric. That intense, burning feeling is fervor. Fervor means intense and passionate feeling. Religious fervor, patriotic fervor, revolutionary fervor. It shares its root with fever: something that burns.

gre.s: The early ____ of the movement gradually cooled into apathy as its leaders became mired in internal disputes.
gre.clue: gradually cooled into apathy

example: The scientist spoke about coral reefs with such fervor that several students switched their majors to marine biology.

en: Very confident, showy, and colorful in a way that attracts attention
hook: FLAMBOYANT: like FLAMES, bright and impossible to ignore.
story: Flamboyant. At the awards night, most guests wore black. Then the singer arrived: a gold jacket, purple feathers on his shoulders, sunglasses studded with sparkling stones, and boots that lit up with every step. He blew kisses to the crowd and twirled for the cameras. Every lens turned toward him. He was flamboyant: confident, showy, and colourful in a way that demands attention. Think of flames, bright and impossible to ignore.

gre.s: Unlike her ____ predecessor, who favored sequined gowns and dramatic entrances, the new director dresses plainly and avoids the spotlight.
gre.clue: who favored sequined gowns and dramatic entrances

example: The flamboyant chess champion arrived at every match in a velvet cape, though his play was cautious and precise.

en: An obstacle; something that blocks progress
story: Impediment. Each monsoon, the only road to Arif's village floods, and the children cannot reach school for weeks. The water is a serious impediment to their education: an obstacle that blocks progress. Arif's cousin also had a speech impediment, a stammer that made job interviews hard until therapy helped. The Latin root ped means foot, as in impede: an impediment shackles your feet. Contrast expedite, which frees them. Synonyms: obstacle, hindrance, barrier.

gre.s: Lack of reliable electricity remains the single greatest ____ to industrial growth in the region, deterring investors who might otherwise build factories there.
gre.clue: deterring investors who might otherwise build factories there

example: Poor eyesight was no impediment to Rafiq's career as a radio host, since listeners only ever heard his voice.

en: Designed to start fires; tending to stir up conflict or anger
hook: INCENDIARY: think INCENSE that's lit, or a fire that's lit.
story: Incendiary. Police found small incendiary devices hidden in a market in Old Dhaka: bottles designed to start fires. A week later, a politician gave a speech so full of hatred that his supporters smashed shops and burned cars that night. The newspapers called it an incendiary speech. Incendiary means designed to start fires, either literally or figuratively. Incendiary words set people's anger on fire. Think of incense being lit, but far more dangerous.

gre.s: The editor refused to print the letter, judging its ____ language likely to provoke riots in an already tense city.
gre.clue: likely to provoke riots

example: The blogger was arrested after posting incendiary videos that urged viewers to attack a neighbouring village.

en: Going on and on without ever stopping
story: Incessant. In July, the rain in Sylhet began on a Monday and did not stop. Not for an hour. Not for a minute. Nine days of steady, drumming rain. Roads flooded, walls grew green moss, and Joya's clothes never dried. Children forgot what the sun looked like. The rain was incessant: continuing without any pause. In means not, cessant means ceasing. Incessant barking, incessant complaining, incessant traffic noise.

gre.s: The ____ noise from the construction site, which continued day and night for months, drove many residents to move away.
gre.clue: which continued day and night for months

example: The incessant honking on Mirpur Road makes it almost impossible to hold a phone conversation near the bus stop.

en: Harmless and unlikely to upset anyone
story: Innocuous. At the family dinner, Sara asked her cousin a simple, friendly question: "So, when is the wedding?" She expected a date and a smile. Instead, her cousin burst into tears and ran upstairs. The engagement had been cancelled that morning. Sara's question had seemed innocuous: harmless and inoffensive. Most garden snakes look frightening but are innocuous. In means not, nocuous means harmful, as in noxious.

gre.s: What seemed an ____ comment about the budget was interpreted by the minister as a direct attack and provoked a furious response.
gre.clue: was interpreted by the minister as a direct attack

example: Most garden spiders are innocuous to humans, though their size frightens many people who find them in the shed.

en: Narrow-minded and uninterested in outside ideas or cultures
hook: INSULAR: like an ISLAND (insula in Latin), cut off from the world.
story: Insular. In one remote village, people distrusted anyone from the next district. New foods were called dangerous. New music was called immoral. Visitors were watched with suspicion until they left. Nothing from outside was welcome. The community was insular: narrow-minded and uninterested in outside ideas or cultures, like an island cut off from the world. Insula means island in Latin. Insular communities often resist change.

gre.s: Critics accused the academic department of being ____, citing its refusal to engage with scholars from other disciplines or countries.
gre.clue: its refusal to engage with scholars from other disciplines or countries

example: Raised in an insular boarding school, Omar knew almost nothing about popular music until he arrived at university.

en: Fearless and adventurous
story: Intrepid. Wasfia Nazreen, a Bangladeshi mountaineer, climbed the highest peak on every continent. Storms tore at her tent. Frostbite threatened her fingers. The air near the summits was so thin that each step felt like a mile. She kept climbing. She was intrepid: fearless and adventurous. In means not, trepid relates to trepidation, meaning fear. An intrepid explorer goes where others are too afraid to go. Its opposite is timorous.

gre.s: The ____ journalist ventured into the war zone that other reporters had fled, sending back dispatches from the front lines.
gre.clue: that other reporters had fled

example: Intrepid divers explored the flooded cave for six hours, mapping tunnels that no person had ever entered.

en: A model of excellence; a perfect example
story: Paragon. In Anika's family, every child was compared to cousin Mahin: top marks, polite to elders, generous to the poor, captain of the cricket team, and he even helped his mother cook. Anika rolled her eyes. "Yes, yes, Mahin is a paragon," she sighed: a model of excellence, a perfect example. Paragon comes from an old Italian word for a touchstone used to test gold. A paragon of virtue is the standard others are measured by. Synonyms: model, exemplar, epitome.

gre.s: Admired throughout her long career as a ____ of integrity, the judge stunned the public when evidence emerged that she had accepted bribes for years.
gre.clue: Admired throughout her long career

example: Our neighbour, a paragon of patience, taught all six of us children to ride a bicycle without once raising his voice.

en: Having a limited or narrow outlook
hook: PAROCHIAL: limited to the local PARISH.
story: Parochial. Uncle Habib has lived his whole life in one neighbourhood of Old Dhaka. He believes the best biryani, the best tailors, and the best people are all within three streets of his house, and he dismisses any idea from outside as foolish. His views are parochial: limited and narrow in outlook. The word comes from parish, a small church district; a parochial mind never leaves its own parish. Synonyms: provincial, insular, narrow-minded. Opposite: cosmopolitan.

gre.s: Critics complained that the festival had become increasingly ____, showcasing only local filmmakers and ignoring the vibrant international cinema it had once championed.
gre.clue: showcasing only local filmmakers and ignoring the vibrant international cinema

example: The newspaper's parochial coverage filled its front page with a council quarrel on the very day a war broke out abroad.

en: A strong liking or habitual tendency
hook: PENCHANT: leaning toward it like a PENDANT hangs down.
story: Penchant. Arif cannot pass a roadside tea stall without stopping. He drinks six cups a day, knows the best stall in every neighbourhood, and plans his walks around them. He has a penchant for tea: a strong liking or habitual tendency. Penchant comes from the French for leaning, so a penchant is something you lean toward. One may also have a penchant for exaggeration or for arriving late. Synonyms: fondness, inclination, proclivity.

gre.s: Given the senator's well-known ____ for theatrical gestures, no one was surprised when he tore up the bill on live television.
gre.clue: no one was surprised

example: Kabir's penchant for puns made him popular at parties and unbearable during exam week.

en: Graceful, calm, self-controlled manner
hook: POISE: perfectly POISED, balanced and calm.
story: Poise. At her first interview at a big bank, Sara's chair wobbled, her pen ran out of ink, and one interviewer asked a deliberately rude question. Sara simply smiled, borrowed a pen, and answered every question calmly and clearly. Later, the interviewer praised her poise: her graceful, calm, self-controlled manner. Poise originally meant balance or weight, like a scale held perfectly level. A poised person stays balanced under pressure. Synonyms: composure, self-possession, grace.

gre.s: Even when hecklers repeatedly interrupted her speech, the young candidate showed remarkable ____, answering each insult calmly and returning to her argument without missing a beat.
gre.clue: answering each insult calmly

example: Only fourteen, the young pianist played before a packed hall at Shilpakala Academy with the poise of a seasoned professional.

en: To prevent from happening; to make impossible
bn: আগেই রোধ করা; অসম্ভব করে তোলা
hook: PRE-CLUDE: CLOSE the door BEFORE it can happen.
story: Preclude. Zayan dreamed of joining the army since he was six. At eighteen, he passed every written exam with top marks. Then the medical test found an old knee injury from a cricket match. The rules were clear: the injury precluded him from serving. To preclude is to prevent something in advance, making it impossible. Pre means before, clude means close: closing the door before you can walk through. His busy schedule precluded any holiday.

gre.s: The patient's weak heart may ____ surgery, forcing doctors to consider gentler forms of treatment.
gre.clue: forcing doctors to consider gentler forms of treatment

example: Dense fog precluded any flights from leaving Dhaka until midday, stranding hundreds of passengers in the terminal.

en: To fill something up again
story: Replenish. The tea stall outside the medical college runs out of almost everything by noon. So every afternoon, Rahim the owner rides his bicycle to the market, buys new tea leaves, milk, sugar, and biscuits, and fills his shelves again before the evening rush. He replenishes his stock: he fills it up again. Re means again and plen means full, as in plenty and plenary. Athletes replenish lost fluids by drinking water. Synonyms: refill, restock, replace. Its opposite is deplete.

gre.s: After the long drought, months of heavy rain were needed to ____ the reservoirs, which had shrunk to a tenth of their usual capacity.
gre.clue: which had shrunk to a tenth of their usual capacity

example: Elephants visit the salt lick every evening to replenish the minerals they lose in the summer heat.

en: Strictness, thoroughness, and accuracy; harsh conditions
story: Rigor. In Mitu's thesis lab, the professor accepted nothing on trust. Every experiment had to be repeated three times, every number double-checked, and every claim backed by a reference. Students grumbled, but their papers were never rejected. The lab was famous for its rigor: strictness, thoroughness, and accuracy. Rigor can also mean harsh conditions, like the rigors of a Himalayan winter. The adjective is rigorous. Synonyms: precision, thoroughness, strictness. Its opposite is laxity.

gre.s: The journal is famous for its ____: every submitted paper is checked by three independent reviewers, and every statistical claim must be reproduced before publication.
gre.clue: every statistical claim must be reproduced before publication

example: Few of the volunteers were prepared for the rigors of a long winter at the Antarctic research station.

en: Willing to cheat or do wrong to get what one wants
story: Unscrupulous. A travel agent in Narayanganj promised fifty families jobs in Malaysia: good salaries, free housing, flights included. Each family paid two lakh taka, some selling their land to do so. One morning the agent's office was empty and his phone was switched off. He had vanished with everything. He was unscrupulous: having no moral principles, willing to cheat anyone. Scruples are your conscience. The unscrupulous have none.

gre.s: The ____ landlord evicted elderly tenants on false pretexts so that he could rent their apartments at triple the price.
gre.clue: evicted elderly tenants on false pretexts

example: Unscrupulous builders sometimes save money by mixing too much sand into the concrete, endangering everyone who will live inside.

en: Built for practical use, with little thought for beauty
story: Utilitarian. The new university hostel had no paintings, no carpets, no decorations at all. Plain concrete walls. Metal bunk beds. Simple wooden desks. Bright white tube lights. But everything worked perfectly: hot water, fast Wi-Fi, strong locks. It was utilitarian: designed to be useful and practical rather than attractive. Think: all about utility. In philosophy, utilitarianism judges actions by how much good they do for the greatest number of people.

gre.s: The factory's ____ design, which prioritized efficiency over appearance, made it one of the least attractive buildings in the city.
gre.clue: prioritized efficiency over appearance

example: Grandfather's utilitarian bicycle had no gears, no bell and no paint, yet it carried him to the market for forty years.

en: Fearing or disliking people from other countries
story: Xenophobic. When a group of foreign workers arrived to build a bridge near a small town, some residents welcomed them with food. Others put up signs saying foreigners go home, refused to sell them rice, and blamed them for every crime. That fear and hatred of outsiders is xenophobic. Xeno is Greek for stranger, and phobia means fear. Xenophobic politicians often blame immigrants for problems they did not cause. Opposite: cosmopolitan. Synonyms: nativist, chauvinistic.

gre.s: Critics warned that the party's ____ rhetoric, which blamed immigrants for every economic problem, would inflame hostility toward the nation's foreign-born residents.
gre.clue: blamed immigrants for every economic problem

example: Some fans shouted xenophobic insults at the visiting team's foreign players, and the league banned them from the stadium for a year.
